state
  1. Inside the acinar cell, trypsinogen (open ring) is activated to trypsin (red dot), a proposed route being lysosomal cathepsin B (mostly rodent data)
  2. Feed-forward: trypsin activates more trypsinogen and the other zymogens
  3. The gland digests itself: acinar injury, then inflammation around the lobule (hover)
  4. Chronic: repeated injury activates stellate cells; collagen builds and acini shrink. Repeated injury also drives ADM, and pancreatic cancer risk is about 12-fold in chronic pancreatitis (pooled; Beger 2023).

Hover or focus a part for a short explanation. Choose Acute: trypsinogen is activated inside the acinar cell, trypsin activates more of it, and the gland digests itself. Choose Chronic: repeated injury activates stellate cells, collagen fills the space and the acini shrink.

Sources

Educational only, not medical advice. On a phone, swipe the figure sideways and tap a part to read about it. Schematic, not to scale; counts, positions and speeds are illustrative and the levels come from a qualitative model, not measurements. Mechanism details come from experimental systems (mostly rodent) and human pathology. No measured number is displayed except those quoted in the hover text from the sources below; all levels in the figure are qualitative.

  • Acute pancreatitis, overview and pathogenesis. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 9th ed., ch. 19 (acute and chronic pancreatitis: acinar injury, premature activation of proenzymes, fat necrosis, fibrosis in chronic disease; page-level facts as recorded in the project's atlas-facts.json, pp. 884-888). Whitcomb DC, Clinical practice. Acute pancreatitis, N Engl J Med 2006;354:2142-50 (doi:10.1056/NEJMcp054958).
  • Histology of acute and chronic pancreatitis. Beger HG et al. (eds), The Pancreas, 4th ed. 2023: ch. 17 (Klöppel, histopathology of acute pancreatitis; 90-95% interstitial oedematous, 5-10% necrotizing; fat necrosis), ch. 38 (chronic pancreatitis), ch. 52 (duct stones) as recorded in the project notes.
  • Cathepsin B and intracellular trypsinogen activation. Halangk W et al., J Clin Invest 2000;106:773-81 (doi:10.1172/JCI9411; cathepsin B-deficient mice, secretagogue-induced pancreatitis: trypsin activity more than 80% lower, acinar necrosis about 50% lower).
  • Ca²⁺-driven activation and vacuoles in the apical pole. Raraty M et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2000;97:13126-31 (doi:10.1073/pnas.97.24.13126; isolated acinar cells, 10 pM CCK did not, 10 nM CCK did, activate trypsin and form vacuoles).
  • Cancer link. Lowenfels AB et al., Pancreatitis and the risk of pancreatic cancer, N Engl J Med 1993;328:1433-7 (doi:10.1056/NEJM199305203282001; 2015 patients with chronic pancreatitis, standardized incidence ratio 14.4, 95% CI 8.5-22.8, with at least 5 years of follow-up; the first cohort value, not the shared figure below). Shared figures: chronic pancreatitis about 12-fold (pooled), hereditary pancreatitis about 69-fold or 25-40% lifetime risk by age 70: Beger 2023 ch. 61 p. 481 (Maisonneuve & Lowenfels); Robbins 9e ch. 19 p. 909. The statement that acute pancreatitis alone adds only a small risk, largely an undiagnosed tumour, comes from an independent literature review and was not re-checked against a primary source. Guerra C et al., Chronic pancreatitis is essential for induction of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by K-Ras oncogenes in adult mice, Cancer Cell 2007;11:291-302 (mouse).
  • Human genetics. Whitcomb DC et al., Hereditary pancreatitis is caused by a mutation in the cationic trypsinogen gene, Nat Genet 1996;14:141-5. Witt H et al., Mutations in the gene encoding the serine protease inhibitor, Kazal type 1 are associated with chronic pancreatitis, Nat Genet 2000;25:213-6.
  • Models. Lerch MM, Gorelick FS, Models of acute and chronic pancreatitis, Gastroenterology 2013;144:1180-93 (doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2012.12.043).
  • Stellate cells and fibrosis. Apte MV, Pirola RC, Wilson JS, Pancreatic stellate cells: a starring role in normal and diseased pancreas, Front Physiol 2012;3:344 (doi:10.3389/fphys.2012.00344). Identification and culture of rat and human stellate cells: Bachem MG et al., Gastroenterology 1998;115:421-32. TGF-β and PDGF as drivers: project notes citing Gorelick and Williams 2021, ch. 1.
  • Acinar cell structure and storage. Pandol SJ, The Exocrine Pancreas, Morgan & Claypool 2010 (NCBI Bookshelf NBK54128). Active versus inactive secreted enzymes: Fieker et al., Clin Exp Gastroenterol 2011; Whitcomb and Lowe, Dig Dis Sci 2007.

Note. Most mechanistic data on the cathepsin B route and on vacuole formation come from rodent or isolated-cell experiments; in humans the trigger varies (for example alcohol or gallstones, about 80% of Western acute pancreatitis per Robbins 9e), and trypsin-independent injury pathways also exist, so the figure shows one well-studied initiating route, not the whole disease.

Simplified. One acinus of three cells in section; the duct tree is shown as a single channel. Trypsin is shown spreading to the base and out of the cell as a stand-in for released enzymes. Stage transitions are qualitative and run in minutes to years in reality. Moved to hover text or omitted: the duodenum and enteropeptidase, oedema, neutrophils and fat necrosis, the capillary, ER and Golgi, duct distortion. Not shown: mitochondria and the Ca²⁺ signal that precedes activation, autophagy and NF-κB signalling, SPINK1 protection in the figure itself, duct obstruction, systemic effects, islet loss, pseudocysts, and the ADM and PanIN steps themselves.
